paragraphs: King Yannai. Hyman writes: In [Berakhot 29a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.29a.6-7) the Gemara relates that Yochanan the High Priest served in the high priesthood eighty years and in the end became a Sadducee. Abaye said: Yannai is Yochanan. Rava said: Yannai is one and Yochanan is another; Yannai was wicked from the outset and Yochanan was righteous from the outset. And although the truth is as Rava said — for Yochanan the High Priest, who is called in the Antiquities John Hyrcanus,

was righteous almost all his days but at the end of his days became a Sadducee, as explained in his entry, and Yannai was his son, who reigned in place of his brother Aristobulus, and he was a Sadducee from beginning to end, as we shall explain — Abaye did not err; he says only that the Gemara also calls Yochanan by the name Yannai, as stated explicitly in [Kiddushin 66a](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.66a.8-11), “It happened with King Yannai,” and Hyman identifies the king in this account with John Hyrcanus,[^10]

as explained at length in the Antiquities, and so it is in Rabad. Hyman writes: I have already explained at length in the entry Yochanan the High Priest that, although he was faithful to the sages of Israel almost all his days, yet the great wars that he waged almost all his days without asking the counsel of the sages of the Sanhedrin, and also because he saw how the sect of the Sadducees was more dangerous than the enemy

without — therefore, for the sake of peace, he drew them near to him and gave them access within his house, and he did not sense in himself how little by little he was swept along by the current of the time until they caught him in their net. But his sons, who were always with the Sadducee leaders in their wars, were raised upon their knees from their youth. As is related in the Antiquities, when Yochanan the High Priest died and commanded that his wife reign in his place, what

did his son Aristobulus do? Not only did he not do his father’s wish, but he did the opposite and killed his mother by starvation — something only a true Sadducee could do, such terrible cruelty. Aristobulus’s wife was the sister of Shimon ben Shetach, known as Queen Shalminon (שלמינון). Aristobulus reigned only one year, and when he died without sons she fell to levirate marriage before his brother; she released

his brothers, who were in prison, and was taken in levirate marriage by Yannai his brother, and he rose to be king and High Priest. Through her wisdom she influenced her husband not to persecute the Pharisees in anger, and therefore her brother Shimon ben Shetach found access to the royal house, even though the whole Sanhedrin consisted of Sadducees, as Hyman says he has discussed at length in the entry Shimon ben Shetach. Through his great wisdom, with the help of his sister, he pushed back little

by little the Sadducees and appointed in their place Pharisees faithful to the Lord and to His Torah, and he sent for his teacher Yehoshua ben Perachyah, who came to Jerusalem, as stated explicitly in [Sanhedrin 107b:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.107b.12). This is what Hyman understands [Kiddushin 66a:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.66a.12) to mean when it says that the world was desolate (from the day Yochanan the High Priest became a Sadducee) until Shimon ben Shetach came and restored the crown to its place. Hyman cites Isaac Hirsch Weiss’s Dor Dor ve-Dorshav (דו״ד), part 1, page 127:

“Alexander Yannai married the widow of Aristobulus, who was his yevamah, as a wife; and although he was High Priest, who is not permitted to marry a widow even when she is his yevamah ([Yevamot 20a:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.20a.8)), he married her before he was appointed High Priest — and in such a case a High Priest is permitted to marry a widow, [Yevamot 61a:6-7](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.61a.6-7)” (his meaning is that he betrothed her before he was appointed High Priest, like the case of Yehoshua

ben Gamla). “And perhaps this event was the reason for the sages to establish this halakhah and to permit Yannai on its basis to marry his brother’s widow” — end of quotation. Hyman replies: With all due respect, he made a great error, for a yevamah who falls before a yavam has no status of betrothal at all, only the status of a wife taken in marriage, as it is written (Deuteronomy 25), “her yavam shall come upon her and take her to himself as a wife”; and at the beginning of Kiddushin, the yevamah is acquired (only)

by intercourse. As for what they said in Yevamot 6:4 (61a) — the rule that if one betrothed a widow and was then appointed High Priest he may take her in marriage — that applies only to a widow from the general public, but not to a yevamah who fell before him. On the contrary, they said there in the Mishnah that a woman awaiting levirate marriage who fell before an ordinary priest, and he was appointed High Priest, even though he performed ma’amar with her, he may not take her in marriage. If so, how can one say that this

event led the sages to establish this halakhah? What halakhah did they establish then? Hyman says the objection that the wife of a king may not enter into levirate marriage presents no difficulty at all: Aristobulus had no status of a king at all, though he called himself king. Hyman cites Rambam, Laws of Kings 1:10 [1:7 in the supplied text], which states that they appoint in Jerusalem only

a king of Israel of the seed of David; and as is related in the Antiquities, Aristobulus himself put the royal crown upon himself and did not take counsel with the Sanhedrin of the sages of the Torah, because then they were all Sadducees. If so, Hyman argues, undoubtedly he had no status of a king. Therefore when he died and his wife inherited the kingship, and by Torah law she fell to his eldest brother for levirate marriage, she released Yannai from prison, he being the eldest

of his brothers (although he was then young, about twenty-two years old, and she was much older than he), and he took her in levirate marriage by Torah law, since he was not yet either king or High Priest. This is clear, Hyman concludes. Now although Yannai was a complete Sadducee, yet, as we said, through the wisdom of Shimon ben Shetach and his sister the queen, the crown was restored to its former state and his teacher Yehoshua

ben Perachyah was brought back, and, in Hyman’s reconstruction, undoubtedly Yehoshua ben Perachyah died in the way of all the earth, and Shimon ben Shetach or Yehudah ben Tabbai sat in his place as Nasi. But afterward there occurred the incident related in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 7:2 and Nazir 5:3: three hundred poor Nazirites came up, and Shimon ben Shetach asked King Yannai to help him with the Nazirites’ sacrifices, for which he needed nine hundred offerings;

he asked that Yannai give half and that he himself give the other half. Shimon ben Shetach, in his great wisdom, found a release for a hundred and fifty Nazirites, and thereby exempted those Nazirites, covering his half of the undertaking. They informed on him to Yannai that he had given nothing of his own, and the king was angry with him, and Shimon ben Shetach fled and hid. In [Berakhot 48a:5](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.48a.5) it is related how Shimon ben Shetach returned to the king’s house, and it is more fully explained in the Jerusalem Talmud

there, 7:2: once great officials from the kingdom of Persia came to Yannai, and when they sat down to eat they asked, “Where is that old man who used always to sit and speak words of wisdom?” The king told them the story, and they asked him to pardon him. His wife, who knew where Shimon was hidden, sent and brought him and seated him between herself and the king. When he asked why he had mocked him in the matter of the Nazirites,

Shimon ben Shetach [supplied abbreviation ח״ש] answered, “I spoke the truth, for you helped with your money and I with the wisdom of my Torah.” “And why did you flee instead of telling me?” Shimon replied, “I heard you were angry with me, and I fulfilled the verse, ‘Hide for a little moment until the wrath passes.’” In [Sanhedrin 19a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.19a.16-17) it is related that once Yannai’s slave killed a person. Yannai was summoned to court to fulfill the verse “and its owner has been warned.” When he arrived, Shimon said to him, “King Yannai,

stand on your feet and let them testify against you.” Hyman continues: Several of the later scholars twist what is straight and say that the slave who killed a person was Herod, who killed Chizkiyah and his men, and that “Shimon ben Shetach” is a scribal error. They themselves erred and needlessly denied an explicit Gemara. In Dor Dor ve-Dorshav (ד״ור), part 1, page 132, Weiss says that according to the Talmud, Shimon ben Shetach was the queen’s brother,

and the halakhah that one’s sister’s husband is disqualified from testifying ([Sanhedrin 27b:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.27b.10)) had not yet been introduced. Otherwise how could he have judged Yannai? One disqualified from testifying is disqualified from judging ([Niddah 49b:17](https://www.sefaria.org/Niddah.49b.17)). Hyman replies: With all due respect, he made a great error. A court of twenty-three sat there, since Yannai’s slave had killed a person, an offense tried by twenty-three. Thus there was a court even without Shimon ben Shetach [reading ב״ד in the print], and he was only

the Nasi; and the rule that he is disqualified from judging applies only if he himself is the judge. This is clear. Likewise it is mentioned at the end of Keritot that King Yannai and the Queen were sitting; the king said a kid is fine and the queen said a lamb is fine. They said, “Let us ask Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai, who is High Priest” — he gestured with his hand. The king said to him, “Since he gestured with his hand, cut off his right hand,” etc.

(Hyman argues: From this too there is great proof that there was always a serving High Priest besides the official High Priest.) Likewise he is mentioned in [Berakhot 44a:5-6](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.44a.5-6). In the Antiquities, end of book 13, once on the festival of Sukkot, when he came to offer the burnt offering (which was then always the greatest rejoicing for the people, and then he displayed his high priesthood and performed the service himself), many of the people threw the etrogim

that were in their hands — and said to him, “Go out, go out, son of a chalalah” — and he killed some six thousand of them. In [Sukkah 48b:2](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.48b.2), in the Mishnah, it is related that once one poured the libation on his feet (in the way of the Sadducees), and all the people pelted him with their etrogim; his name is not mentioned, and likewise they said in the Gemara at [Sukkah 48b:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.48b.12), “It happened with a certain Sadducee.”[^11] In Jerusalem Talmud Sukkah 4:6 they say

that that Sadducee also committed another transgression, [ומה; unresolved supplied word], and so it is cited in the Tosefta there, chapter 3. But in Sefer ha-Kabbalah of Rabad this incident is related of King Yannai — Alexander. Hyman concludes: From this we see the great righteousness of our holy Rabbis, who did not wish to mention this great disgrace of the house of the Hasmoneans, through whose fathers a great salvation was wrought for Israel.

It is related in the Antiquities that in his lifetime he killed fifty thousand innocent men of Israel. Once, when he grew weary of his internal wars, he asked the people how he might reconcile with them, and they all answered that only at his death would they rejoice. In Megillat Taanit, chapter 1 [as Hyman cites it], it is related that when King Yannai fell ill, he sent and seized seventy of the elders of Israel, shut them up in prison, and commanded

the prison warden to kill the elders if he died, so that while Israel rejoiced over him they would grieve over their teachers. They said: Yannai had a good wife named Shalminon. When he died she took his ring from his hand and sent it to the warden so that he would free the elders. Hyman writes that the Gaon Rabbi Shlomo Yehudah Leib Rapoport [ר״ש רפפורט] rightly remarked, in Erekh Millin, page 64, that a scribal error fell into Megillat

Taanit, and it should read “when Herod fell ill,” and the woman is Salome, Herod’s sister, who saved the elders from death; only because the printers did not know of Herod’s sister and knew that Yannai’s wife was named Shalminon, they wrote the name Yannai in place of Herod. And the truth is so, Hyman argues, for how could one say this of Yannai and his wife Shalminon — is it not known that after Yannai’s death his wife

Shalminon reigned, for so he commanded before his death? Likewise it is explained in [Sotah 22b:6](https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.22b.6) that King Yannai said to his wife: “Do not fear the Pharisees, nor those who are not Pharisees, but the hypocrites.” And in the Antiquities it is related that he repented before his death and commanded his wife to strengthen the hands of the Pharisees, and for this they gave him great honor at his death and forgot all the evils he had done to them all the days of his life.

Hyman concludes: He died at forty-nine years of age, having reigned twenty-six years [supplied כו׳], and after him his wife Shalminon reigned nine years, and in her days were the best days for Israel in all the days of the Second Temple.

notes.text: Whole supplied Hebrew/all28 English line-group units/all current and historical substantive notes/Fable proposals reviewed. Hyman owns the Yannai/Yochanan identifications, dynastic chronology, Sadducee judgments, levirate-marriage and royal-status arguments, appointments and strong clear/undoubtedly/always assertions; these are translated with their force and attribution, not adopted as canonical history or legal rulings. Source queen שלמינון is Shalminon, restored rather than silently harmonized to Shelamzion; the saved Warsaw1874 MegillatTaanit Shevat scalar writes שלמינין. Herod’s sister Salome remains a separate person. Aristobulus’s wife and Yehoshua benPerachyah’s death antecedents made explicit. ופטרן refers to the150 Nazirites whom Shimon exempted, confirmed by whole Guggenheimer JTBer7:2 selected paragraph; it does not say he exempted himself. Supplied כ״ד is24, restored against the draft’s22, while the same argument first gives a23-person court: this inconsistency remains held without guessing an intended numeral. Supplied ח״ש is shown alongside contextual ShimonbenShetach, supported by named JTBer7:2, but no damaged-letter or printed-pixel claim is admitted. The isolated ומה is restored visibly and held. Source Rambam Kings1:7 is retained alongside the matching rule in named ToratEmet363 chapter1 scalar9 (1:10); source MegillatTaanit chapter1 is retained alongside the saved Shevat story. Neither comparison proves a printed correction or its history. Hyman and Rapoport’s proposed Herod substitution and accusation about printers remain attributed proposals; the saved MegillatTaanit text actually says Yannai. Source books דו״ד/ד״ור and Rapoport’s abbreviated given name remain disclosed rather than independently resolved. Final reign numeral כו׳ is shown as supplied with the26-year reading; no unread Josephus witness is claimed to settle it. The Antiquities refers to Josephus; Hyman’s reported narratives and final age49/queen9years are preserved, not independently verified against Josephus. All historical source questions, original notes and versions preserved. Digital editions are not printed pixels or correction-history proof.

Hyman treats two different proposed Herod identifications differently: he rejects substituting Herod in the slave-trial narrative, while accepting Rapoport’s proposed Herod substitution for the imprisoned elders story. These are distinct passages, not a single blanket identity decision. The saved Megillat Taanit witness continues to say Yannai; Hyman’s account of a printers’ substitution remains his attributed explanation.

Kiddushin 66a calls the king Yannai in the story about the challenge to his priesthood. Ibn Daud, in the Neubauer edition of Sefer ha-Kabbalah, pp. 52–53, tells a related story about Yochanan, whom he calls the first Hyrcanus, and calls Alexander his son Yannai. Sanhedrin 107b has Shimon send to Yehoshua ben Perachyah when peace returns. The Jerusalem Talmud accounts of the Nazirites in Berakhot 7:2 and Nazir 5:3 have Shimon sit between the king and queen after he is summoned. The queen brings her brother in the parallel in Bavli Berakhot 48a. Keritot 28b calls Yissakhar High Priest in the story. The conclusion about two simultaneous holders of that office is Hyman’s.

The etrog accounts differ. Sukkah 48b gives an unnamed pourer in the Mishnah and calls him a Sadducee in the Gemara. The consulted Tosefta text gives a Boethusian in brackets. Jerusalem Talmud Sukkah 4:6 reports competing ways of linking the incidents. Ibn Daud names Alexander and describes a student striking him with an etrog. Josephus, Antiquities 13.372–373, describes the crowd pelting Alexander as he was about to sacrifice and reports about six thousand deaths. At 13.376 he places at least fifty thousand deaths in a six-year conflict. At 13.401–405 he gives the king’s advice to entrust power to the Pharisees and Alexandra’s action on that advice. Hyman characterizes the advice as repentance.

At Antiquities 13.404, the consulted Greek edition gives twenty-seven years of rule and fifty-one years of life. The displayed Whiston and Rogers translations give forty-nine years of life. Hyman’s supplied text gives twenty-six years of rule and forty-nine years of life. Josephus gives Alexandra nine years of rule at 13.430. The supplied reading of Hyman stands. The cited passage in Rapoport’s Erekh Millin, p. 64, remains unverified in the cited edition.

Isaac Hirsch Weiss’s Dor Dor ve-Dorshav, part 1, printed p. 127, discusses Alexander Yannai’s marriage to Aristobulus’s widow before his elevation to the high priesthood and suggests that the event might have prompted the rule. Hyman condenses the passage and adds his interpretation about betrothal. Yevamot 61a distinguishes prior betrothal to a widow from a widow awaiting levirate marriage, even after ma’amar. The cited Kiddushin passage has Shimon restore the Torah to its former state. The “crown” is Hyman’s phrasing.

The printed Hyman (vol. II, p. 767) cites halakhah 10 (ה״י), while the supplied Hebrew reads ה״ז. The Torat Emet edition of Laws of Kings 1:10 has the rule about appointing a king of Davidic descent in Jerusalem. Hyman applies the rule to Aristobulus.

The supplied speaker abbreviation is ח״ש. Shimon ben Shetach gives the reply to Yannai in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 7:2 and Nazir 5:3. In those versions he comes upon being summoned and sits between the king and queen. The queen explicitly brings her brother in Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 48a.

Weiss, Dor Dor ve-Dorshav I, p. 132 n. 2, proposes that the rule disqualifying a sister’s husband had yet to be established. Hyman disagrees. After explicitly writing “twenty-three” earlier in the sentence, the Hyman print (p. 768) gives ב״ד, “a court,” where the supplied Hebrew has כ״ד. Sanhedrin 19a–b names Yannai, his slave and Shimon ben Shetach, without specifying the tribunal’s number. Hyman’s characterization of who served as judge belongs to his argument.

The isolated ומה is present in the Hyman print (p. 768), as is his Megillat Taanit chapter 1 reference. The consulted Warsaw edition has the elders’ story in Shevat and names Yannai. In the Prague 1852 edition of Erekh Millin, printed p. 64, Rapoport cites the opening of chapter 11 and proposes reading Herod in place of Yannai and identifying the woman as Herod’s sister Salome. He compares Josephus’s report involving Salome and her husband Alexas. The account of the printers’ reasoning is Hyman’s.

The printed text on p. 769 gives כו׳ in the phrase about the length of the reign, read here as twenty-six years. In the consulted editions of Josephus (Antiquities 13.404), the Greek gives twenty-seven years of rule and fifty-one years of life. The Whiston and Rogers translations also give twenty-seven years of rule, with forty-nine years of life.

[Berakhot 29a:6–7](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.29a.6-7) gives the disagreement between Abaye and Rava. [Kiddushin 66a:8–11](https://www.sefaria.org/Kiddushin.66a.8-11) names King Yannai. [Seder HaDorot 1808](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=1808&lang=en) quotes Yuchasin’s identification of the Yochanan who became a Sadducee with Hyrcanus I, also called Yannai. Hyman distinguishes the historical figures and uses the shared name to explain Abaye’s wording.

In Kiddushin, Shimon ben Shetach restores the Torah to its former state. Hyman says “the crown.” Yevamot distinguishes betrothal before appointment as High Priest from a widow awaiting levirate marriage. In the Hebrew of Sukkah the Mishnah leaves the pourer unnamed and the baraita calls him a Sadducee. Hyman’s identification draws on the other accounts discussed above.
